title: Two material directions. One engineered structure.
summary: Carbon for the performance prototype; fiberglass for a possible recreational derivative. Both begin with a designed sandwich structure and a clear estimate boundary.
dateLabel: 04 Oct 2026 · source review; document date not stated

sections.title: The proposed direction
sections.text: The materials report proposes a carbon-composite performance prototype focused on low mass, with fiberglass as a possible route to a more accessible recreational board. Both use epoxy and structural foam sandwich construction as the estimating basis. No laminate design, structural equivalence or production quotation has been established.

sections.title: How the sandwich works
sections.text: Two composite skins are separated by a lightweight structural core. The separation helps the panel resist bending, while the bond between skins and core must transfer load. Structural foam is a working part of the panel, not simply filler. Core grade, thickness, resin system and local load paths need to be selected together.

sections.title: Each material needs its own design
sections.text: Carbon is the proposed minimum-mass route; fiberglass is the lower-cost direction. Matching ply count does not establish equivalent structure. Fibre orientation, panel span, impact response, core behaviour and reinforcement all matter. A fiberglass shell with local carbon is a third candidate, but material transitions and additional processing may offset some of its benefits.

sections.title: Compare finished hulls on the same basis
sections.text: The source ranges below include deck, bottom, rails, a hatch allowance, core, skins, bonded joints, local reinforcement, inserts and finish. They exclude engine, starter, exhaust, pump, battery, electronics, fuel system, fuel, fins, footpads and straps. Assign the engine cradle and pump support consistently to either hull or equipment before comparing totals.

sections.title: Where the central mass allowances come from
sections.text: The illustrative carbon budget totals 5.5 kg: 2.8 kg for fibre and resin, 0.8 kg for core and associated bonding, and 1.9 kg for local reinforcement, joints, inserts and finish. The fiberglass budget totals 8.0 kg: 5.1 + 0.8 + 2.1 kg. The 2.5 kg difference is a planning comparison, not a measured prototype result.

sections.title: The geometry belongs to an earlier estimate
sections.text: The report carries forward an earlier assessment of 28_for chatgpt.3dm: approximately 1.77 m length, 0.572 m maximum width, 0.229 m overall vertical envelope and 1.97 m² external surface area. It does not independently recalculate them. They are not substituted for current H0 study geometry. Overall height is not engine-bay clearance, and exterior area is not total fabric purchasing area.

sections.title: A reproducible estimating shortcut
sections.text: Skin mass = area × combined dry fibre mass per area × (1 + resin-to-fibre mass ratio). The source uses 1.97 m² once, with all plies across both skins included in the fibre allowance. Carbon: 1.97 × 0.80 × 1.78 ≈ 2.81 kg. Fiberglass: 1.97 × 1.40 × 1.85 ≈ 5.10 kg. These assumed fibre allowances and resin ratios are not a build-ready laminate or proof of equal strength. Inner and outer areas are approximated as equal.

sections.title: Cost is more than fabric
sections.text: The source assumes an established mould and a small series of about 20–50 hulls. The total allowances cover materials, consumables, fabrication, bonding, trimming, finishing and routine inspection. They exclude tooling, engineering, development tests, freight, tax and supplier profit. Prototype fabrication and an actual outsourced purchase price may differ substantially.

sections.title: What the saving can—and cannot—mean
sections.text: The central comparison is US$1,100 for carbon and US$800 for fiberglass: US$300, or about 27%, less hull manufacturing allowance. This is not a guaranteed saving. In the report’s illustrative whole-board scenario, the hull is assumed to be 40% of a US$2,750 carbon manufacturing budget. Keeping US$1,650 of other costs unchanged gives US$2,450 for fiberglass, a total reduction of about 10.9%. The 40% share is a project assumption, not an industry benchmark.

sections.title: A recreational price ambition
sections.text: The document sets a future US$4,000–5,000 retail ambition for the recreational board. It is not an announced selling price or an available offer. Freight, applicable tax, distribution, warranty, support, overhead and development recovery still need to fit. The difference between retail price and manufacturing allowance is not profit. Tooling also needs separate recovery: the report’s hypothetical US$10,000 tool would allocate US$500 across 20 saleable hulls, US$200 across 50 or US$100 across 100.

sections.title: Design the concentrated loads
sections.text: Detailed work must cover rider and landing loads, hatch perimeter and seal, engine vibration, pump thrust and alignment, intake, rail joints and attachment points. Fasteners need engineered local load transfer rather than reliance on unreinforced foam. Penetrations and bonds need protection against water ingress. A common exterior does not guarantee identical internal tooling or assembly for both materials.

sections.title: The evidence needed next
sections.text: Trial the material and process to measure cured mass, resin uptake and bond quality. Check mounts, inserts, joints, hatch fit and leakage on structural assemblies. Then measure complete-board mass and CG and assess handling, temperature, vibration and durability under defined conditions. Acceptance criteria must be agreed before testing. Neither construction has completed this validation in the supplied record.

sources: Report references: Gurit Guide to Composites and Core Materials Brochure support general sandwich principles; they do not validate Wahoo estimates.
changes: Initial materials website record. Source diagram redrawn without a background panel; comparison charts reproduce source ranges. Planning allowances and commercial scenarios are preserved as estimates, with exclusions. Original document unchanged.

title: Place the fuel. Control the change.
summary: A low tank ahead of the engine, close to the intended centre of gravity: balance and independent service access guide the current direction.

sections.title: A mass that changes during the ride
sections.text: The current direction is a relatively flat, elongated tank, low in the hull and immediately ahead of the engine. Its fuel centroid is intended to remain close to the target longitudinal centre of gravity (LCG). The aim is to limit balance changes as fuel is consumed while retaining access for service. Final capacity, dimensions, material and installation coordinates are open.

sections.title: A working window, not a frozen station
sections.text: The supplied fuel study proposes an LCG window of approximately 38–42% of hull length forward from the transom. It is a starting hypothesis for the complete mass model and prototype tests. The source layout graphic is schematic and its marker does not align with that numerical window. This redraw follows the stated transom datum; it does not derive a tank position from the original picture.

sections.title: Distance matters as well as mass
sections.text: Fuel has a moment arm about the rest of the system’s centre of gravity. Keeping its centroid nearby reduces the contribution of fuel consumption to CG migration. Placing it farther forward or aft increases that contribution for the same fuel mass. The final answer depends on the engine, exhaust, pump, hull, battery, other equipment and rider—not on the tank alone.

sections.title: Why proximity reduces migration
sections.text: For a fixed non-fuel assembly, combined CG = (non-fuel mass × its CG + fuel mass × fuel centroid) / total mass. The example below isolates that relationship using dimensionless inputs. Rider stance is held fixed and the fuel centroid is assumed constant; neither is necessarily constant during a real turn.

sections.title: Handling remains a question for testing
sections.text: The intended benefits are controlled trim, predictable corner response and consistent intake presentation as fuel burns. The source discusses stern squat, planing and porpoising, but supplies no measured comparison or dynamic model. Those benefits are objectives to evaluate; the static mass equation cannot demonstrate them.

sections.title: Remove the tank. Keep the engine installed.
sections.text: Independent tank removal is a packaging requirement. Reserve a usable access opening, disconnection points and a clear extraction path. Baffles and/or fuel-compatible foam are under consideration to control slosh. Pickup behaviour, venting, thermal expansion and fittings must be resolved with the selected fuel system.

sections.title: Capacity follows the duty cycle
sections.text: The newer engine report defines 15–20 minutes of racing and 40–45 minutes of leisure operation as requirements. Neither is demonstrated endurance. Its fuel-flow and tank-size examples are illustrative, so they are not adopted as Wahoo capacity. Final usable volume must come from consumption logs and pickup performance in the intended duty cycles.

sections.title: The next evidence
sections.text: Build the complete mass model for full and low fuel, include rider stance and actual internal geometry, and inspect vertical as well as longitudinal CG. Then evaluate the installed prototype. The earlier H0 R03 level-immersion calculation remains a separate study and does not validate this layout.

title: A defined baseline. Interfaces still open.
summary: The latest engine report selects the 54 × 54.5 mm direction and a Wössner component route, while leaving manufacturing dimensions subject to verification.

sections.title: What has advanced
sections.text: The 4 October engine report retains Option A: 54.00 mm nominal bore and 54.50 mm stroke, giving a calculated 124.817 cc. It records the 8160DA single-ring piston and CS2018 complete crankshaft strategy as the project baseline, with P2018-family rod references. These are project selections, not supplier approval for Wahoo or evidence of tested marine durability.

sections.title: The axes define the packaging problem
sections.text: With the crankshaft aligned to the pump, the horizontal cylinder lies approximately across the hull. Its cylinder-axis stack uses local interior width. Bearings, crank webs, shaft ends and the coupling use length along the pump axis. The maximum outer hull width cannot establish the engine bay’s usable space.

sections.title: The nominal dimension chain
sections.text: Use r = 27.25 mm, L = 102 mm and H = 28 mm as the report’s working geometry. At top dead centre, crown-datum reach is r + L + H = 157.25 mm; at bottom dead centre it is L − r + H = 102.75 mm. Rod centre distance and the supplier’s crown datum must be confirmed. Neither reach is the complete engine width.

sections.title: Piston and pin need their own datums
sections.text: The report identifies 8160DA as the single-ring baseline and WP032 as the pin reference, listed at 15 mm OD, 10 mm ID and 45 mm length. A 28 mm compression-height reference remains conditional on its crown datum. These are source-report references pending drawings or exact-part inspection; the diagram deliberately avoids inventing the crown or skirt.

sections.title: The rod reference is not an optimum
sections.text: A 102 mm rod gives L / stroke ≈ 1.872 and L / crank radius ≈ 3.743. Increasing rod length changes angularity and packaging together; it does not guarantee a power gain. The source’s Ø29 and Ø19 eye references include space for bearings and must not be mistaken for crankpin or gudgeon-pin diameters.

sections.title: Design around the purchased crank
sections.text: The CS2018 sourcing route replaces the earlier custom-crank assumptions. Do not carry the old assumed 100 mm web, 25 mm journals or bearing-centre spacing into the new crankcase. Obtain the actual journals, shoulders, shaft ends, pack width, rotation and sweep first. The report also flags inconsistent main-bearing designations to resolve before machining.

sections.title: What we buy and what we develop
sections.text: The proposed split retains matched purchased moving parts and traceable bearings, then develops the crankcase, cylinder, head, exhaust and installation interfaces around verified data. Pump thrust needs its own deliberate load path. Component prices and a piston-plus-crank subtotal are not a complete engine cost, so the website makes no production-cost claim.

sections.title: A release requires evidence
sections.text: The immediate milestone is a verified piston–rod–crank interface package: supplier drawings or commissioned metrology of identified parts. Confirm crown volume, ring-pin paths, masses, runout, fits and bearing details. No machining tolerances, coating process, squish clearance or service interval is released by this baseline.

changes: Source-reviewed website edition. Diagrams redrawn for the website; source originals retained. Nominal calculations and schematic relationships are not manufacturing releases or measured performance.

title: From crank angle to piston travel.
summary: Reproducible nominal geometry explains motion and packaging. It does not establish power, durability or a finished port map.

sections.title: One revolution, calculated
sections.text: The source model is a rigid, zero-offset slider crank with a 27.25 mm crank radius and 102 mm rod centre distance. These plots are recalculated from those inputs at the 12,000 rpm design reference. One revolution lasts 5 ms. The reference speed is not a validated operating limit.

sections.title: Mean and peak speed answer different questions
sections.text: Mean piston speed is total travel per unit time: twice the stroke multiplied by revolutions per second. It is 21.80 m/s at 12,000 rpm. The instantaneous peak is approximately 35.45 m/s. The curves exclude bearing clearances, deflection and thermal growth; neither value is a strength or fatigue assessment.

sections.title: Why a shorter stroke saves less than expected
sections.text: The report compares Option A with a hypothetical 56 × 50.6 mm configuration using the same 102 mm rod and 28 mm compression height. The crown-datum reach falls from 157.25 to 155.30 mm: a saving of 1.95 mm, not 40 mm. A hypothetical 25 mm compression height would bring that reach to 152.30 mm, but it is not an approved parts combination. Overall package width still includes the case, head and service space.

sections.title: The crown determines the head relationship
sections.text: The selected piston’s actual crown contour is unresolved. Flat, domed and dished examples explain why a photograph is insufficient for head design. Clearance volume and squish depend on the real crown, deck datum and hot assembly. A head gasket alters the head relationship; a base gasket also moves the cylinder ports relative to the crank.

sections.title: Port timing starts with motion and geometry
sections.text: A port roof is uncovered when the actual piston edge passes it. Under a matching flat-datum assumption, required travel is roof depth below deck minus the piston’s TDC deck clearance. The report’s worked opening angles are examples only. No port widths, heights or timing settings are selected for production.

sections.title: Beyond opening angle
sections.text: Effective area through the cycle, gas pressure, transfer direction, ring support and the exhaust all matter. A geometric opening event alone cannot specify a working cylinder. The next record needs the actual crown and ring-pin paths, a controlled port map and a tested engine/exhaust combination.

changes: Source-reviewed website edition. Diagrams redrawn for the website; source originals retained. Nominal calculations and schematic relationships are not manufacturing releases or measured performance.

title: Air, fuel, cooling—and the installed engine.
summary: The new engine report keeps injection and lubrication open, compares cooling architectures, and sets a staged route to measured results.

sections.title: Keep the prototype lessons traceable
sections.text: The report records Max’s observations from the earlier Rotron XT100 installation: changes to port timing, gasket thickness, exhaust and intake-air provision, including a second snorkel. The exhaust change was reported as particularly noticeable. Original measured geometry and dyno traces are not included, so these remain reported development observations.

sections.title: Air has a route of its own
sections.text: The proposed reed-inducted architecture supplies air through the crankcase and transfer ports. Upstream, transfer-port and direct-cylinder fuel injection remain options. Selecting direct injection would not remove the need for scavenging air. If fuel and oil bypass the crankcase, the bearings need a separately engineered oil route.

sections.title: The exhaust belongs in the engine study
sections.text: Port events, pipe geometry, temperature and pump load must be developed together. Preserve and measure the earlier pipe before treating its reported success as a design input for the larger engine. The report releases no tuned length, cone angle or power curve.

sections.title: Cooling is now an explicit comparison
sections.text: The September brief proposed pump-fed raw water. The newer report compares that with an isolated coolant loop and states that neither is selected. Raw water exposes engine passages to the service environment; an isolated loop adds a heat exchanger, circulation pump, hoses and coolant mass. Reserve the complete envelope before releasing housings.

sections.title: Oil, water and starting need installation tests
sections.text: Both fresh- and salt-water operation are requirements. The horizontal arrangement needs verified oil delivery, drainage, hot restart and anti-ingestion measures. Brushless starting requires measured cold/hot cranking demand and coordinated motor, controller, reduction, freewheel and pack. The report’s example electrical loads do not size a battery.

sections.title: Measure before committing to production
sections.text: The sequence begins with exact-part metrology, then dry assembly, leak and flow checks, controlled starting, instrumented dyno work, representative endurance and installed-hull tests. Record build identity, clearances, fuel/oil, ECU calibration, exhaust revision, conditions and instrumentation. Preserve raw data as well as presentation plots.

sections.title: Close the loop with teardown
sections.text: Use wear, sealing, bearing, fastener and temperature evidence to guide the next build. Race and leisure endurance must reproduce their load histories, not only elapsed time. No universal temperature threshold, torque band or service interval is asserted before component guidance and testing establish it.

title: An engine is only the beginning.
summary: A horizontal two-stroke, its waterjet and everything between them: the V1 brief starts with the complete installation.

sections.title: The newer component baseline
sections.text: The 4 October engine report now identifies a component sourcing baseline. Read the updated engine record; the September brief below remains part of the history. Cooling alternatives and open injection decisions are covered in the new integration article.

sections.title: The starting brief
sections.text: The September V1 brief calls for a nominal 125 cc, single-cylinder, horizontal two-stroke with electronic fuel injection and brushless electric starting. These are design requirements. Power, torque, installed mass and the engine-to-pump drive ratio are not established specifications.

sections.title: Built around the corner exit
sections.text: The ambition is 70 km/h with an 85–90 kg rider, alongside predictable throttle pickup and strong acceleration out of tight turns. The speed is an unverified target. The rider range is a design input, not a certified payload. The brief does not ask for 70 km/h through every sharp turn; it asks for controllable drive and repeatable recovery as the board straightens.

sections.title: Match the internals. Engineer the interfaces.
sections.text: The source strategy is to evaluate a compatible purchased piston, cylinder, head and crank family together. Custom work then concentrates on packaging and interfaces. A displacement label alone cannot establish fit: the exhaust envelope, shaft line, cooling connections and removal paths all belong in the same installation study. This record does not release a supplier or part number for purchase.

sections.title: Fuel, air and heat share the space
sections.text: Injection location remains an integration decision. Air routing must account for water separation. The exhaust needs both its tuned volume and a workable thermal envelope. Jet-pump-fed cooling is proposed, but its circuit has not been defined in this brief. Bilge removal is a separate function and must not be confused with the cooling or propulsion circuits.

sections.title: A correction worth keeping
sections.text: The historical output drop near 11,000–12,000 rpm came from an engine-only dynamometer test: no jet pump was moving water. The register records the quantity as probably torque, with the original graph still needed. It is not evidence of pump cavitation, a proven engine-speed limit or a diagnosis of the cause.

sections.title: How this connects to the hull
sections.text: This brief predates the current H0 R03 website studies and references an earlier Rev27 packaging envelope. Those revision systems are independent. The next integration record needs actual component envelopes, masses, centres of gravity and service clearances against the chosen hull geometry.

title: Test the opening. Then the mechanism.
summary: Fixed nozzle comparisons come first. A moving conical pin is a conditional next step, with geometry that can be examined before performance is claimed.

sections.title: Start with fixed areas
sections.text: The whitepaper retains a fixed-nozzle test gate: compare a baseline and two alternative outlet areas before committing to an active mechanism. Engine and pump matching, launch response, corner exit and speed need repeatable measurements. A smaller outlet is not automatically a faster board.

sections.title: Three positions, one outlet
sections.text: The WJ70-C01 concept summary describes a non-rotating conical pin translating inside a fixed circular outlet. As a wider part of the cone reaches the exit, the open annulus shrinks. The proposed Ø48 mm outlet and Ø10, Ø15 and Ø20 mm pin sections give the three positions below. All dimensions are provisional.

sections.title: What the numbers mean
sections.text: Open area = π × (outlet diameter² − pin diameter²) / 4. The proposed end positions reduce the exit area by approximately 13.6%. This is a geometric calculation. It predicts neither flow rate nor thrust, efficiency, cavitation or top speed. Travel is measured from the concept’s P0 reference; the sketch is an exit view, not the full cone.

sections.title: Clearance is not a tolerance
sections.text: The same study uses a 70 mm rotor and proposes a 70.6 mm liner bore. Their difference corresponds to 0.30 mm radial clearance on each side. That is not a ±0.30 mm manufacturing tolerance or an approved running clearance. Rotor integrity, deflection, thermal effects and manufacturing control still need review.

sections.title: Keep the development gate
sections.text: After fixed-area testing, the proposed sequence is locked pin positions, followed by active movement only if evidence supports it. Guidance, sealing, actuator load, position feedback and mechanical stops remain integration questions. No launch-versus-top-speed control strategy has been validated.

sections.title: Scope of this record
sections.text: The whitepaper summarises a separate six-sheet WJ70-C01 drawing package. Those drawings were not supplied for this website review. The circles here are calculated from the whitepaper’s exit dimensions; they are not a reproduction or verification of that CAD package. Impeller blade-count and helical variants also remain concepts, not demonstrated improvements.

title: Make starting part of the design.
summary: A removable electrical pack and brushless starter belong in the board architecture from the beginning.

sections.title: Newer integration record
sections.text: The October report adds starter-duty and installed-engine validation scope. Read the follow-up. Its illustrative electrical loads are not selected battery ratings.

sections.title: Access without opening the engine bay
sections.text: The V1 requirement is an externally accessible battery cartridge: remove it, charge it separately and replace it with a spare without opening the main engine bay or handling loose cables. The service objective is defined; the physical dock is not a released design.

sections.title: One starting system
sections.text: The brushless motor, controller, gearing, freewheel, battery and protection must be specified together. Voltage, chemistry, capacity, cranking demand and charging time remain open. This is an electrically started petrol board; the battery is not the propulsion energy source.

sections.title: The interface matters
sections.text: The dock study must resolve keyed contacts, retention, water protection and safe removal. Injection, ignition and accessories add continuous demand beyond starting. The electrical architecture needs a load budget and protection strategy before a pack can be selected. The brief does not establish hot swapping.

sections.title: Visibility and rider control
sections.text: A red rear visibility light is required in the brief; a removable front light is optional. These do not establish a certified navigation-light system or approval for night operation. Rider-control concepts in the archive provide design context, while the final control logic and hardware remain to be validated.

title: Turn the brief into evidence.
summary: The next chapter connects sourcing, fit, bench work and water testing. Each answers a different question.

sections.title: Begin with a traceable baseline
sections.text: The project register separates requirements, proposals and unresolved decisions. The immediate task is a matched component shortlist, supplier information and an installation envelope. A collection of individually plausible parts is not yet a compatible assembly.

sections.title: Fit before fabrication
sections.text: A digital installation study should check clashes, heat, shaft alignment, structure and service access. A proposed half-scale, non-running mock-up can examine assembly and proportions. Neither CAD fit nor a printed mock-up establishes durability or performance; this record does not claim that mock-up has been built.

sections.title: Bench work has its own questions
sections.text: The engine and pump need defined operating ranges and measured behaviour before combined conclusions are made. Record engine speed and pump speed separately. Preserve test setup, calibration and the measured quantity so that a torque curve cannot later be mistaken for a pump result.

sections.title: Water testing closes a different loop
sections.text: The brief calls for repeatable launch, throttle pickup, corner exit and straight-line speed assessment. Rider mass, fuel state, water conditions, hardware and calibration must accompany comparisons. Numerical acceptance criteria for response still need definition. The 70 km/h ambition remains a target until measured under a documented procedure.

sections.title: Keep optional studies in their place
sections.text: Alternative fin positions are deferred. A wing appears as an exploratory idea in the earlier booklet, with no demonstrated benefit. The V-tail is a required design direction, but its handling benefit is not established. None of these labels proves the current H0 hull has already satisfied the brief.

sections.title: Read revisions by subject
sections.text: Whitepaper Rev04 extends the nozzle concept. Register Rev04 preserves the engine-only dyno clarification. The booklet is Rev01 and is based on Whitepaper Rev03. They are complementary records, not three equally current specification releases; none supersedes the later H0 R03 numerical study simply because it carries a higher revision number.

title: What keeps the hull afloat?
summary: How requested mass changes the level hull’s immersion in still water—and what this calculation cannot tell us.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: How far does the hull settle into still water as the requested mass increases? The H0 R03 displacement study evaluates freshwater at 998 kg/m³ and seawater at 1,025 kg/m³, with pitch and roll held at zero.

sections.title: What the calculation shows
sections.text: At a requested mass of 40 kg, the calculated level immersion in seawater is approximately 0.0705 m. At 80 kg it is approximately 0.1318 m. These are samples of a level-attitude displacement curve, not equilibrium solutions for a particular rider or component arrangement.

sections.title: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The model is a sealed external envelope. Openings, intake and seals are not modelled. The 100 kg request is unachievable in both source series and is omitted from the plotted curves. No uncertainty band is supplied. This is not a physical test, dynamic performance result or safe-payload rating.

sections.title: What comes next
sections.text: Actual loaded equilibrium cases require fuel capacity, fuel density and liquid centre of gravity, plus rider mass, stance and body centre of gravity. Clearance to real openings must also be assessed before operational conclusions are drawn.

sections.title: The starting point
sections.text: The project archive contains layout drawings and renders showing an earlier complete-board concept. They capture the relationship between the deck, handles, internal packaging and outer shape.

sections.title: Why preserve it?
sections.text: A development record should retain the alternatives and earlier stages, not replace them every time a new model appears. These assets show a previous design direction. Their exact dates and relationship to physical prototypes are not yet confirmed.

sections.title: From concept to evidence
sections.text: The current website places these archive assets alongside the H0 engineering studies. The historical board renders and current hull are different records; they should not be read as a measured before-and-after performance comparison.

title: First, establish the reference.
summary: A consistent coordinate system makes later measurements easier to compare.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: Before comparing hull sections or centre-of-gravity positions, the direction and origin of the measurements need to be explicit. The reference-verification archive documents top, side, bow and stern views.

sections.title: The convention
sections.text: The Wahoo reference uses +X forward, +Y port and +Z up. Engineering stationing and physical geometry are distinct: a stationing datum must not be used to flatten or replace the shaped stern.

sections.title: Check the side projection
sections.text: The recorded bow, stern and beam points are shown against native surface samples in the same R01 coordinate frame. Position and height can be inspected together, including the raised bow. The original annotated sheet provides the orthographic native rendering and full verification context.

sections.title: Check the end projection
sections.text: The Y/Z view makes the port-positive convention explicit. Points from different longitudinal locations project onto this same view, so the bow marker is not an aft cross-section point. Selected points and bounding-box corners have different meanings.

sections.title: The stern pick was not the aft-most point
sections.text: The R01 selected reference length was 174.82 cm, while the native longitudinal bounding span was 177.35 cm. An actual native surface sample lay about 25.07 mm aft of the selected stern. That observation established a reference question, not a need to repair the shape. Later R02 stationing is a separate record and should not be silently substituted into R01 drawings.

sections.title: What this establishes
sections.text: This record supports a consistent description of the hull. It is a reference check, not evidence of hydrodynamic performance or a physical acceptance test.

sections.title: Next steps
sections.text: Keep subsequent source revisions and coordinate conventions attached to each published measurement so comparisons can be checked.

changes: Expanded with three sampled reference projections and original R01/R02 annotated verification drawings. Native surface samples are displayed in their recorded R01 frame.
